newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Albright sets U.S. conditions for NATO membership.
newsitem.headline: Albright sets U.S. conditions for NATO membership.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright Thursday set out her country's priorities for new NATO members and made clear that Washington would prefer to keep the first-round of post-Cold War expansion limited to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

In remarks to a NATO foreign ministers meeting that formally discussed for the first time candidates for alliance expansion, she said the new members must meet the highest possible standards before joining and must be able to contribute to NATO's common security.

Although Albright did not say so explicitly in the written statement, her remarks were meant to underscore the U.S. view that only Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic should be invited to join NATO when the alliance's 16 leaders meet in Madrid July 8-9.
Romania and Slovenia have also pushed hard for admission but Washington wants to keep them for a second round.

"The United States does see some advantage in a smaller group" because Poland, Hungary and the Czech republic meet the high standards Albright spotlighted and it would more easily ensure NATO will expand in the future," a senior U.S. official said.

In her presentation to the ministers, Albright declared that NATO "must continue to insist that the candidates for membership in NATO meet the highest possible standards before they are invited to join."

"The alliance should admit only those new democracies that have both cleared the highest hurdles of reform and demonstrated they can meet the full obligations of membership ... NATO enlargement is not a scholarship programme," she said.
"We want the first round of enlargement to be seen as a solid success in these terms and we want to be backed by strong parliamentary and public majorities," she said.
France has pushed hard for Romania's admission and the Ameicans agree Bucharest has made strides since a democratic election last year.

But Washington, concerned Romania's democracy must be given more time to prove its staying power, wants to see more economic and political reforms. There is also concern Romania could not pay its share of NATO expansion costs.

Slovenia, backed by Italy and others, is more stable and democratic and would be better able to pay its way as in NATO. U.S. officials have not explained why Slovenia should not be admitted now, except to say leaving it out would increase pressure for a second round of expansion.

With these and other NATO aspirants in mind, Albright said "we must make a clear and credible commitment in Madrid to those nations that are not yet ready for membership...They need to be certain that there is no invisible barrier across the open door we have pledged".

To this end, she said "it is essential that NATO begins a new phase of dialogues with aspiring countries after Madrid (because this would be) the most clear signal of NATO's intentions on enlargement in the years ahead".
Some argue that after Madrid, NATO should take a pause -- even as much as a few years -- before considering another round of new members.

Albright said: "We cannot promise any country that it will one day join NATO. But we can offer a process that gives substance to the commitments we have made, one that helps aspiring nations understand what they must do and how they must change to make membership a possibility."

After NATO ministers met for several hours, the senior U.S. official said "obviously there is not a consensus yet" on expansion. He also said "not all NATO members have accepted" the strong U.S. insistence that NATO maintain an "open door" to further enlargement.

He said President Bill Clinton, who was visiting London on Thursday, had not yet taken a final decision on what ex-Warsaw Pact states to back as NATO's first post-Cold War members, a point that gives Washington some room to manoeuvre in case a groundswell of support builds for Romania and/or Slovenia.

Regardless of what NATO leaders decide in Madrid, the U.S. Senate and other legislatures in the 16 alliance capitals will have the final say on expansion and Albright stressed the need to "bring our legislators into this process." She also cautioned "we have to be serious and forthright about the costs of enlargement", estimated in the billions of dollars.
